short.speaker: Abigail Adams
short.text: I desire you would Remember the Ladies…
short.source: Abigail Adams to John Adams, Braintree, 31 March 1776

short.speaker: Abigail Adams
short.text: …not paid to the Laidies we are determined to foment a Rebelion
short.source: Abigail Adams to John Adams, Braintree, 31 March 1776

short.speaker: John Adams
short.text: As to your extraordinary Code of Laws, I cannot but laugh.
short.source: John Adams to Abigail Adams, Philadelphia (reply to 'Remember the Ladies'), 14 April 1776

short.text: Thomas Jefferson named the conversation “The United States of America”
short.source: Interface gag for the Declaration of Independence, adopted by Congress 4 July 1776 (Jefferson drafted it)

short.speaker: Thomas Jefferson
short.text: He is vain, irritable … This is all the ill which can possibly be said of him.
short.source: Thomas Jefferson to James Madison, Paris (about John Adams), 30 January 1787

short.speaker: Benjamin Franklin
short.text: …in this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.
short.source: Benjamin Franklin to Jean-Baptiste Le Roy, 13 November 1789

short.speaker: John Adams
short.text: I always loved Jefferson, and still love him.
short.source: Remark made aloud to Edward and John Coles at Quincy; relayed in Jefferson to Rush (5 Dec 1811) and copied by Rush to Adams (16 Dec 1811), summer 1811

short.speaker: Thomas Jefferson
short.text: "I always loved Jefferson, and still love him."—this is enough for me.
short.source: Thomas Jefferson to Benjamin Rush, 5 December 1811

short.speaker: John Adams
short.text: You and I ought not to die, before We have explained ourselves to each other.
short.source: John Adams to Thomas Jefferson, 15 July 1813

short.speaker: Thomas Jefferson
short.source: Deathbed account recorded by Dr. Robley Dunglison (variants by Nicholas Trist and Thomas Jefferson Randolph), evening of 3 July 1826
Jefferson died at Monticello in the early afternoon, 4 July 1826

short.speaker: John Adams
short.source: Reported deathbed words at Quincy (family accounts and contemporary reports; discussed around John Quincy Adams's July 1826 diary), 4 July 1826
